clue.text: The sort of treatment one should have at one's fingertips

definitions.text: The sort of treatment one should have at one's fingertips

parts.words: The sort of treatment one should have at one's fingertips
parts.note: having something at one's fingertips usually means knowing it well, but here the treatment is literally applied to the fingertips and nails

explanation.surface: A remark that some kind of therapy ought to be second nature to you.
explanation.definitionFit: A beauty treatment for the hands and nails is given right at the fingertips.

clue.text: Potentate acting to break up demonstration

indicators.note: to break up says one piece interrupts the other, splitting it

parts.note: a march is a protest demonstration
on means acting or performing, as an actor on stage

explanation.surface: A powerful ruler acts to disperse a protest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'demonstration' suggests a show of something, but here it is a protest march; 'to break up' splits it.
explanation.definitionFit: A potentate is a ruler with great power, such as a sovereign king or queen.

clue.text: Birmingham station welcomes opening of shop and paper stall

indicators.note: welcomes means takes in, so the station abbreviation holds a letter

parts.note: New Street, abbreviated New St, is Birmingham's main railway station

indicators.note: opening of picks the first letter of the word shop

explanation.surface: A Birmingham railway station takes in a new shop and a stall selling papers.
explanation.walkthrough: Birmingham New Street is the city's main railway station, usually written New St; 'welcomes' lets the shop's first letter in before the St.
explanation.definitionFit: A kiosk selling newspapers and magazines is a paper stall.

clue.text: Johnson is holding ring to polish

indicators.note: holding means the two pieces either side grip a letter between them

parts.note: Dr Samuel Johnson was nicknamed the Great Cham, cham being an old word for khan or ruler
taken as written
a ring is round, like the letter O

explanation.surface: Dr Johnson is holding a ring so that he can polish it.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Johnson, the 18th-century compiler of the Dictionary, was called 'the Great Cham of literature'; 'holding' means the letter sits between the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft leather from the goat-antelope is used to buff surfaces, so as a verb it means to polish.

clue.text: Mischievousness of those whose pictures are on show in gallery

definitions.text: those whose pictures are on show in gallery
definitions.meaning: a rogues' gallery is a police collection of photos of criminals, so the second sense is rogues collectively

explanation.surface: Naughtiness from the people whose portraits hang in a gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: A rogues' gallery is a police collection of mugshots, so the people pictured are rogues.
explanation.definitionFit: Knavish or playfully naughty behaviour is mischievousness, and the word can also mean rogues collectively.

clue.text: Run out and meet one's death

definitions.meaning: a ticket or lease that runs out comes to its end date
to meet one's death is to die

explanation.surface: Someone's time ends twice over: a contract lapses and its holder dies.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share the idea of coming to an end: a passport lapses, a person breathes their last.

clue.text: Lines may be produced thus without reaching any conclusion

definitions.meaning: in geometry a line may be produced, that is extended, forever
never coming to a stop or final point

explanation.surface: A geometry teacher on how lines can be drawn on and on forever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Produced' is the geometer's word for extended.
explanation.definitionFit: A line drawn on forever, never stopping, is extended without limit.

clue.text: A top honour the old man pockets for medical breakthrough?

indicators.note: pockets means puts away inside, so the old man holds the other pieces

parts.note: pa is a familiar word for father, the old man
N for north sits at the top of a map
in bridge the ace is the highest honour card

explanation.surface: Dad pockets a high award for a medical advance.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: a cure-all would indeed be a breakthrough. Treating 'top' as north, at the top of a map, is a stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A supposed cure for every illness would be the ultimate advance in medicine.

clue.text: Immediate answer from king that is put in mail

parts.note: R is short for rex, Latin for king

indicators.note: put in says the mail word is set inside the abbreviation for that is

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
post is mail, letters delivered

explanation.surface: A quick reply from the monarch has been sent by post.
explanation.walkthrough: POST goes between I and E, after R.
explanation.definitionFit: A riposte is a quick, sharp retort, originally a fencing return thrust.

clue.text: Trendy viewpoint held by unorthodox few in North Dakota

indicators.note: the remaining pieces sit inside the state abbreviation, between its two letters

parts.note: ND is the postal abbreviation for the US state of North Dakota

indicators.note: unorthodox means unconventional, so the word few is put into an unusual order

parts.note: an angle is a point of view on a subject; held by only says it belongs with the jumbled few, joined on after them

explanation.surface: A fashionable opinion is held by a few eccentric people in a northern US state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unorthodox' rearranges few, and 'held by' is only a link joining the viewpoint on; 'in' then sets the lot between the two letters of the state.
explanation.definitionFit: Newfangled describes something new and modish, often with a sneer, matching trendy.

clue.text: When a person conceals part of neck

indicators.note: conceals says the answer lies hidden inside the run of words before it

explanation.surface: A person hides a bit of their neck, perhaps with a scarf.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across wheN A PErson.
explanation.definitionFit: The back of the neck is a specific part of it, so the term names one region.

clue.text: Act precipitately and charge criminal accessories?

definitions.meaning: to act rashly, like a horse taking jumps too fast
a punning reading: rush means charge at, and fences are receivers of stolen goods, accessories to crime

explanation.surface: Someone rashly decides to prosecute the people who helped commit a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: A fence is slang for someone who buys and sells stolen goods. The idiom comes from hunting, where a rider takes the fences too hastily.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to tackle something too hastily, as an eager rider charges jumps.

clue.text: Unconvincing evidence of bits of corn in animal fodder

indicators.note: in places the corn pieces inside the fodder word

parts.note: hay is dried grass fed to livestock
ears are the seed-bearing heads of cereal plants such as corn

explanation.surface: A dubious account of what grain was found in the cattle feed.
explanation.definitionFit: Second-hand report rather than direct testimony is weak evidence, inadmissible in many courts.

clue.text: Vigilance of porters holding up excited redhead

indicators.note: holding means the porters word contains the other pieces

parts.note: porter is a dark beer, so porters are ales
the head, or first letter, of red is R

indicators.note: up in a down clue says the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: sent is slang for thrilled or excited

explanation.surface: Railway porters stay watchful while holding up an excited red-haired person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reads the excited word upwards, giving TNES, which follows the head of red inside the porters.
explanation.definitionFit: Alertness is watchfulness, being on guard, just as vigilance is.

clue.text: A phoney journalist full of remorse

parts.note: a sham is a fake, something phoney
ED, short for editor, is the crossword's usual journalist

explanation.surface: A fake reporter is overcome with regret.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling guilt or shame over something done is being full of remorse.

clue.text: Beggar wrongly named in court, in short

indicators.note: wrongly says the letters of the pieces are set out in a mistaken order

parts.note: CT is the short form of court, as in street names

explanation.surface: A beggar was wrongly identified in court, briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram pool is NAMED, IN and CT together.
explanation.definitionFit: A mendicant lives by begging, as did the mendicant friars.

clue.text: Corporation ban badly restricts Millennium project

indicators.note: restricts means confines, so the jumbled letters are wrapped round the project
badly signals the word ban is to be arranged wrongly

parts.note: the Millennium Dome in Greenwich was Britain's flagship project for the year 2000

explanation.surface: A big company's ban is badly hemming in the government's showpiece millennium scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' makes ABN from ban. 'Corporation' is jocular old British slang for a pot belly.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporation is old humorous slang for a paunch, so it means the belly.

clue.text: Native American creature seen in port of New York

definitions.meaning: the bison of the North American plains
a city in New York State, a port on Lake Erie

explanation.surface: An animal native to America spotted in a New York harbour city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Native American' suggests a people, but here it means native to America. The city is in New York State, not New York City.
explanation.definitionFit: The American bison is commonly called by this name, and Buffalo, NY, is a Great Lakes port.

clue.text: Ring outside another ring is less dark

parts.note: a ring is round, like the letter O

indicators.note: outside says the word for less goes round the second ring

parts.note: minus means less, as in subtraction
a second circle shape, another letter O

explanation.surface: A ring circling another ring looks less gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is less dark' reads as a comparison, but 'less' is the minus sign and 'dark' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ominous clouds are dark and threatening, foreboding trouble.

clue.text: Spray most of shrub with last of insecticide

indicators.note: most of means the shrub's name loses its final letter

parts.note: syringa is the mock orange or the lilac, a garden shrub

indicators.note: last of picks the final letter of the word insecticide

explanation.surface: Instructions for treating a bush with the dregs of a pest killer.
explanation.walkthrough: SYRINGA (lilac or mock orange) loses its final A to 'most of', and the E from the end of insecticide follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To spray with a fine jet of liquid, as gardeners once did with a hand pump, is to syringe.

clue.text: English eccentric often found on beach

indicators.note: eccentric means odd or off-centre, so the word is rearranged

explanation.surface: Odd Englishmen are commonly seen at the seaside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' looks like a description of an English person but signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Shingle is a mass of small pebbles typical of many British beaches.

clue.text: Died in desert, having collapsed showing extreme effects of heat

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation for died inside the jumbled letters
having collapsed suggests the word desert has fallen to pieces and been rebuilt

parts.note: d. is the standard abbreviation for died, as in obituaries

explanation.surface: Someone died in the desert after collapsing from heatstroke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having collapsed' turns DESERT into REDEST, and 'in' puts D inside it after RED.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin or metal grows ever more red as heat increases, so the most extreme heat shows the most red.

clue.text: Principal supports urge to be intellectual

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece supports another by sitting below it

parts.note: to egg someone on is to urge them
a head is the principal of a school

explanation.surface: A headteacher encourages pupils to be intellectual.
explanation.definitionFit: An egghead is a bookish, highly intellectual person.

clue.text: Moderately good tune by piper's son involved in music-making

indicators.note: involved in says the tune and son are wrapped up inside the music-making word

parts.note: fiddling is playing the fiddle, making music

indicators.note: by means beside, so the son follows the tune

parts.note: an air is a melody
Tom, the piper's son, is the pig-stealing boy of the nursery rhyme

explanation.surface: A decent melody by the son of a musician, involved in a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom, Tom, the piper's son' is an English nursery rhyme about a boy who stole a pig.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means passable or reasonably good, neither excellent nor bad.

clue.text: Enlightened circle surrounding a star?

parts.note: an enlightened circle sounds like an intellectual clique round a celebrity, but it is a literal ring of light, round a saint or a heavenly body

explanation.surface: A clique of clever people forms around a celebrity.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring of light seen round the sun, moon or a saint's head is a lit circle.

clue.text: Overstate rejection of food price after cut-back

indicators.note: after says the food and price come behind the turned cut
back attached to cut says the word for cut is turned round

parts.note: to axe something is to cut it

indicators.note: rejection turns the food word away, reading it backwards

parts.note: an egg is a basic food
a rate is a price charged

explanation.surface: Someone protests that food was refused because its cost went up after spending cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut-back' gives EXA and 'rejection of' gives GGE; 'after' puts the turned food and the price behind the turned cut.
explanation.definitionFit: To exaggerate is to make something seem bigger than it is, to overstate it.

clue.text: Some are grey, but they're white in the main

definitions.text: Some are grey, but they're white in the main

parts.words: Some are grey, but they're white in the main
parts.note: in the main seems to mean mostly, but it means on the sea, where breaking crests are called white ones

explanation.surface: A remark that, while a few are grey, most are white.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is poetic for the open sea; white horses are foam-crested waves.
explanation.definitionFit: Grey is a coat colour of these animals, and foaming wave crests are called white ones.

clue.text: Again declared political community insolvent

annotationWithheld.why: Again declared political community insolvent (8): STATE inside RED, but 'insolvent' must both give RED (in the red) and signal the container, one word doing two jobs
